newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Poor Q2 for manufacturers in Australia's NSW - study.
newsitem.headline: Poor Q2 for manufacturers in Australia's NSW - study.

text.p: Manufacturers in Australia's most populous state, New South Wales, reported lower production and weakening profitability in the June quarter, an Australian Business Chamber/Colonial State Bank survey found.
The survey also found that over the next 12 months, NSW manufacturers expected to reduce their worforce by a net 2,500.
"The expectation of cutting jobs stems from the commercial realities being faced by business," Australian Business Chamber managing director Philip Holt said in a statement.
"For most firms, general business conditions continued to deteriorate in the June quarter," Holt said.
The survey, which covered 503 firms, found companies experienced falls in production, sales, profits and selling prices in the June quarter.
"The manufacturing sector continues to exhibit weakness," Colonial State Bank chief economist Hans Kunnen said.
"Apart fron those companies benefiting from expansion in construction and mining, most manufacturers saw a decline in production and profitability," he said.

Larger firms reported better business conditions than smaller firms, and the outlook was more positive for the September quarter with one third of all firms looking for increases in sales, orders and production.

Against that, Holt said that "while a significant majority of firms continue to expect general business conditions to improve in the future, this has also been the case in all recent surveys and in each case those expectations have been dashed by commercial reality."
However, flow on effects from lower interest rates and the building recovery were helping the outlook for the sector.
The expected fall in employment was the eleventh quarterly survey in a row in which the majority of firms had expressed an intention to cut jobs.

Only firms with up to 20 employees expected to increase employment over the next year, but Holt said experience had shown a tendency of business to be hopeful and positive on expectations for profitability and production.
"Therefore, the scenario for employment, even in the small sector, is not of strong growth but is more likely to be one of decline," Holt said.
Falls in selling prices in the March and June quarters were seen as one less obstacle to further rate cuts.

"Given the stability of selling prices and competitive pressures to see them fall, lower interest rates become a real possibilty," Kunnen said, adding this would lift consumer spending and cut borrowing costs.
